column1: # Construction and identity observations (#845); each test implements every id.
# java/rust are the expected observations; - means no counterpart, and note gives the reason
# and the invariant that replaces it. Values are shared only where a row states one contract.

column4: note
Parser.get(Class) twice / one OnceLock<SharedGrammar>::get_or_init twice (Arc::ptr_eq)
Parser.newInstance(Class) / share_grammar(build()) per call
Parser.get(Supplier) with one supplier instance / one OnceLock
two supplier lambdas building equal parsers / two OnceLock statics
Parser.getSupplier(Class) closures delegate to the class singleton / closures calling one accessor
a failing constructor is not cached: Java FactoryBoundCache stores only results; Rust sets the OnceLock only after Ok
ParserFactoryByClass.get(kind,Class): same key, other kind, no kind / one OnceLock per (grammar, kind) key
Java ClassAndKind(Class).kind() is Optional.empty (was Optional.of(null) -> NPE). Rust has no runtime node kind: the kind-less key is the plain factory row

a constructor taking Parsers(ItsOwnClass) re-enters the synchronized factory. Rust must not re-enter OnceLock::get_or_init for the same cell: std leaves it unspecified and the current implementation deadlocks, so it is not executed. Cycles use Rule(index), see lazy-construction-cycle
LazyChoice child Parser.get(Self) / Expr::Rule(own index), parse ((x))
getLazyParsers calls / OnceLock builder calls after three parses on the shared graph

createParser calls / OnceLock builder calls after three parses on one graph in fresh contexts. Java: a user parser that inherits AbstractParser.parse runs the body its createParser builds (#1007); Rust keeps that body in a OnceLock beside the immutable grammar, shared by the graph's contexts

the body builder fails on its first call: nothing is published and the next parse builds it again and succeeds. Java: createParser throws, the delegate field stays unset; Rust: the builder panics inside OnceLock::get_or_init, which leaves the cell empty
createParser runs once, but createParserAndThen runs on every getParser call, also after the first (three parses). Rust has no per-call hook; the OnceLock builder runs once (lazy-delegate-built-once)

the delegate's children before use, after a failed creation, after the first and the second parse, and the body's parent. The first use attaches the body once, a graph change (#1007). Rust has no child list or parent pointer: the body stays outside the rule vector

a children walk begun before the first use finishes on the list it started with (0 children; the attachment replaces the list instead of changing it in place, which threw ConcurrentModificationException), a new walk sees the body. Rust grammars are immutable, so no walk observes an attachment

createParser reads its owner's getChildren (0, before the attachment), getRoot and a name lookup under the owner's reentrant monitor. Rust must not re-enter OnceLock::get_or_init for the same cell (see eager-construction-cycle); its builder reads only the immutable grammar

createParser calling its own getParser recurses, as before #1007: the delegate is published only when creation returns. Rust must not re-enter get_or_init for the same cell (std leaves it unspecified and the current implementation deadlocks), so it is not executed

single-thread graph mutation after the first use: clearing the delegate's children keeps the cached body, which still parses and is not attached again (creations stay 1); the cache lives as long as the parser. Rust rebuilds a grammar to change it (by-name-late-registration)

a name lookup into the body before its first use misses, after getParser() it hits. By-name does not cache the miss (by-name-late-registration), but a ReferenceParser keeps it (predicate-miss-cached), so a frozen graph creates its delegates' bodies before sharing. Rust names resolve at construction and never see a lazily built body
one shared graph, three fresh contexts x! / y / x?
ParserNameContext with two distinct parsers named Item / RuleNames::new([.., Item, Item])
one parser under two parents is one entry (Java fixed in #845) / one rule referenced twice by Rule(index)
ParserNameContext.get / RuleNames::get for an undeclared name
Java default names are class names, so two WordParsers collide. Rust literals are unnamed; only Rule names enter RuleNames
ReferenceByNameParser resolves the first parser in flatten preorder (Item:a before Item:b), inputs a / b. Rust rejects the duplicate in RuleNames; the port chooses the first declaration explicitly

ReferenceByNameParser does not cache a miss, so a parser named Late added after parse 1 is found / rebuilding rules with a new table re-resolves the name. A hit and the root are cached (by-name-hit-cached, root-cache-after-reparent)
ReferenceParser caches its miss for the instance lifetime / the Expr resolved once is kept when rules are extended
predicate evaluations during later parses in fresh contexts: Java caches the first lookup, Rust resolves at construction
Referencer.AbstractReference searches from the root on every call / a lookup function over the current rule vector
RuleNames::reference rejects an undeclared name at construction. Java has no strict lookup; its tolerant miss is the Missing alternative of cases.tsv (reference_or_never)
RuleNames::share rejects rules built out of the declared order. Java parsers carry their own names, so there is no index order to check
a shared singleton's parent is the last container constructed. Rust rules have no parent pointer; dynamic parents are RuleStack frames
findFirstToParent stops after 1000 parents. Rust has no parent walk; unbounded rule recursion is a resource_limit in both (left-recursion row)
A ::= A 'x' through a name reference: Java throws ParseLimitException ULX-PARSE-DEPTH-LIMIT (1024 active frames), Rust returns the non-recoverable rule-nesting resource_limit (256)
PseudoRootParser rejects setParent. In Rust any rule index can be the parse root
PseudoRootParser parses only a single child. Rust roots are one Expr::Rule(index)
AbstractPropagatableSource.getInvertMatchToChild before any parse / a fresh context's token_mode(); Rust keeps the mode per context, never on the shared graph
getInvertMatchFromParent without a source ancestor / token_mode().invert at the root
a leaf under NotPropagatableSource after parse / Custom parser under invert_match reading token_mode().invert
Parser.isTokenParsedBySpecifiedParser(token, exact class / superclass) / Node.rule == rule index / other index
ParsersSpecifier.contains by exact class / a set of rule indices
GrammarRule.nameOf: explicit, ItemParser class default, WordParser, null and blank overrides fall back to the class. Rust Rule.name is always explicit

ParserPrinter simple / detail / mostDetail over the static parent path / an output adapter over the failure RuleStack of Root ::= Item; Item ::= 'x' on y: innermost rule, rule path, path with start CPs. Rust has no parent path or class names, so the values differ

Name.of(fqcn) vs Name.of(Class); Name.classBaseOf vs Name.of(fqcn); Name.of(text) is interned / RuleNames::new rejects two declarations of the fqcn spelling; lookup compares text (an owned String finds the same index). Rust names are text only, so distinct Java kinds need distinct spellings
HasChildrenParser.newFiltered drops a direct child c, parse ab / Vec::retain on the sequence
newWithoutRecursive drops c at any depth keeping each combinator type (Java fixed in #845), parse ab / recursive Expr filter
ChildOccurs of WordParser / ConstructedSingleChildParser (MatchOnly) / Chain with one child; Rust: an adapter over the Expr variant of Literal / MatchOnly / Sequence with one element

Outer ::= Scope; Scope ::= '(' Scope ')' | Item | 'x' with Item ::= 'a' outside the scope, inputs a / (x) on one graph then a on the control without the scope, each in every memo x diagnostics mode. Java: ScopeChoice implements RootParserIndicator, so getRoot() of a ReferenceByNameParser below it is the scope; Rust: the scope is its own grammar with its own RuleNames, called from the outer grammar, so Item is never registered in the scope table
the same scope with ReferenceParser.of(Name) (findFirstFromRoot from the scope) / a position lookup over the scope's declared names only
the effective root seen from a reference below the indicator, and whether findFirstToParent reaches Outer / the root rule of the scope grammar, and whether the scope table resolves Outer

findParents, getPath, ParserHierarchy.isRoot and ParserPrinter detail stop at the indicator (Outer and PseudoRoot are not listed). Rust rules have no parent pointer; the static boundary is the scope's own rule vector (rows above) and the dynamic path is RuleStack (root-indicator-rule-stack)
failure RuleStack of the scoped Outer on y under DETAILED: the indicator bounds static lookup only, both keep the caller frames

Java AbstractParser.parserByName caches a hit per instance: after an earlier Item:b is inserted, the old reference still parses b / a as false/0 / true/1, a reference created afterwards resolves Item:b. Rust: the grammar shared by one table keeps its Rule IDs; a change builds a new grammar whose reference resolves b

Java AbstractParser.getRoot() caches the root at first use: re-parenting a parsed graph under NewRoot (which has Late) keeps the miss; the control is attached before its first parse. Rust: a rule resolved against its own table keeps the never-match when composed into a larger grammar; the control resolves against the larger table

an ID belongs to the table that issued it: a body built with [Use, Item] (Item = 1) reused in a rebuilt [Use, Other, Item] passes share (in range, names in order) and now names Other, so b / a parse true/1 / false/0. Rebuilding needs new references. Java parsers hold object references, so there is no index to go stale

RuleNames::share rejects Expr::Rule(2) from a three-rule table inside a one-rule grammar; unchecked share_grammar turns it into an ordinary failure, so the choice silently falls back to 'x' on ax. Expr::Custom bodies are not inspected. Java has no index

ClassAndKind(null, Class) and ParserFactoryByClass.get(null, Class) fail in the key hashCode (existing behavior, null is not accepted). The kind-less key is ClassAndKind(Class) / Parser.get(Class) (class-and-kind-without-kind, factory-kind). Rust keys are Option<kind>, so None is the kind-less key and there is no null
ClassAndKind(Class) equals another kind-less key, not (Other, Class); (Other, Class) keys are equal / the factory-kind cells keyed None, None vs Some(Other), Some(Other) twice (Arc::ptr_eq)

Chain(Choice Nested(a, c, z), b, c) without c keeps the outer Chain and the nested Choice with their names, inputs ab / zb / cb. Rust keeps the Sequence and Choice variants; inner expressions have no names (a named part is a Rule, which the filter does not enter)
createWith copies neither tags nor other parser metadata (existing behavior): the nested Choice tagged T has no tag after the filter. Parser tags are tracked by #851. Rust Expr has no parser tags

cutting the only child of Commit fails while the filtered graph is built (before #845 the parent replaced its children with copies of itself instead); cutting the Commit itself parses b. Rust's port returns a construction error for the emptied Expr::Commit

original CST of Chain(ZeroOrMore(a)) on aa with createMetaOn / createMetaOff, then Chain(LazyZeroOrMore(a)) with createMetaOff: Transaction.commit keeps a LazyInstance token although MetaFunctionParser tokens are dropped. Rust has no meta-token setting or LazyInstance; this is the meta-function boundary (#851)

a LazyChain implementing StaticParser and Initializable: Parser.get(Class) twice returns one instance, parses m, and initialize() is never called (the factory calls are commented out). ParserInitializer has no caller either. Rust has no marker types

a parser writing parse-local state (Java global scope map / Rust ParseContext::set_state) into the first context; a fresh context on the same shared graph starts without it and parses a. The graph holds no capture, scope or user state
